## Methods

Materials and Synthesis
Chemicals. All chemicals are of analytical grade and used without further purification. Polyvinyl pyrrolidone (PVP, molecular weight of 360,000) was purchased from Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China); sodium borohydride (NaBH4), ethanol, bismuth nitrate pentahydrate (Bi(NO3)3·5H2O) and ferric nitrate nonahydrate (Fe(NO3)3·9H2O) were obtained from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China). The deionized water was supplied by a Millipore system (Outlet water resistivity > 18 MΩ cm at 25 ℃) in all experiments.

Preparation of Bi@Fe2O3 spherical Nanostructures. In a typical procedure, 10 mmol of urea was dissolved in ethylene glycol (EG) under continuous Ar purging. Subsequently, 0.5 mmol of Fe(NO3)3·9H2O was added under stirring for 2 h, obtaining solution A. Additionally, 1 mmol of Bi(NO3)3·5H2O was dispersed in 100 mL EG in a three-necked flask equipped with a reflux condenser, thermometer, and gas inlet/outlet. An appropriate amount of polyvinyl pyrrolidone (PVP) was then added. The mixture was ultrasonicated for 30 min and then vigorously stirred for 1 h. Ar was continuously bubbled through the system for an additional 1 h. The reaction mixture was heated to 150 ℃ and maintained for 4 h under an Ar atmosphere. After cooling to 70 ℃, the resulting solution was marked as solution B. Subsequently, solution A was added dropwise into solution B under Ar atmosphere. After addition, the reaction was maintained at 150 °C for 8 h under continuous stirring and Ar flow. Then, the mixture was cooled to room temperature and allowed to stand for several hours. The obtained mixture was washed sequentially with ethanol and deionized water, followed by vacuum drying at 60 ℃ for 12 h. The dried powder was then transferred into a tubular furnace and annealed at 250 ℃ for 4 h under Ar atmosphere with a ramping rate of 1 ℃/min. The final product, Bi@Fe2O3, featuring a core@shell architecture, was obtained. By varying the amount of Bi(NO3)3·5H2O precursor, a series of samples with different Bi (1-Bi@Fe2O3, 3-Bi@Fe2O3, 5-Bi@Fe2O3, and 7-Bi@Fe2O3) were synthesized accordingly.

Preparation of Fe2O3 catalyst. Pristine Fe2O3 sample was synthesized under identical conditions but without adding the Bi precursor. All products were stored in a desiccator before further characterization and catalytic evaluation.

Preparation of Bi-Fe2O3 flat Nanostructures. Fe(NO3)3·9H2O (2 mmol) and urea (6 mmol) were dissolved in 40 mL of deionized water and subsequently treated hydrothermally at 120 ℃ for 2 h, obtaining FeOOH precursor. The precursor mixture was washed, dried, and calcined at 350 ℃ in air for 2 h to obtain crystalline Fe2O3. Then, 100 mg Fe2O3 was dispersed in 50 mL EG with PVP under ultrasonication. After N2 purging (30 min), Bi(NO3)3·5H2O (0.5 mmol, dissolved in 5 mL EG) was added, followed by dropwise addition of NaBH4 (0.1 M, 10 mL) at 80 ℃. After stirred for 2 h, the mixture was washed alternately with ethanol and water, then vacuum-dried at 60 ℃. Finally, the dried mixture was annealed at 250 °C for 1 h under flowing Ar with a ramping rate of 2.5 ℃/min to stabilize the Bi nanoparticles.

Fundamental characterizations
The powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) spectra were acquired on a PANalytical X’pert MPD Pro diffractometer with Ni-filtered Cu Kα radiation (λ = 0.1538 nm, 40 kV  40 mA). The microcrystalline structure and surface characteristics were examined by a JEOL JSM-7800F field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM) and an FEI Tecnai G2 F30 S-Twin transmission microscope (TEM). The energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analysis was performed using the installed energy-dispersive X-ray detector, OXFORD MAX-80. SEM and EDS images were recorded on the XL-30 ESEM-FEG Scanning Electron Microscope. XPS measurements were conducted using a Kratos spectrometer (Axis Ultra DLD) with monochromatic Al Kα radiation (hν = 1486.69 eV). The in situ XPS was recorded using United States-Thermo Fisher SCIENTIFIC ESCALAB 250Xi. The X-ray source was an aluminum target (Al Kα line energy of 1486.69 eV after monochromator filtration), and the detection pressure was 2 × 10−8 Pa. The UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectrum (DRS) was acquired using a Hitachi double-beam UV4100 UV-vis-NIR spectrophotometer equipped with an integrating sphere in which BaSO4 acted as the background. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) measurements were performed on a Bruker A300 spectrometer.

Ultrafast spectroscopy characterization
Femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy was carried out using a PHAROS PH2 Femtosecond laser system. The excitation source was a Ti:sapphire regenerative amplifier (LIGHT CONVERSION, Lithuani, 35 fs pulse width, 1 kHz repetition rate, 3 mJ per pulse). The output beam was divided into two paths to feed a pair of optical parametric amplifiers (TOPAS-C) for generating the pump and probe pulse. A white light continuum (350–950 nm) was produced by focusing the 1300 nm signal from one OPA (TOPAS1) onto a sapphire plate, then filtered with a short-pass filter to limit the spectral window. The pump pulses at 560 and 870 nm were generated from the second OPA (TOPAS2), with fluences adjusted to 5.0 mJ cm–2 and 0.7 mJ cm–2, respectively. Temporal resolution was achieved by introducing a delay line into the pump beam path, allowing the capture of differential transmission spectra over time. To correct for spectral dispersion in the white light probe, the optical Kerr effect of the substrate was measured following a standard polarization-resolved method. This involved setting the pump polarization at 45° relative to the probe and analyzing the probe polarization changes after transmission through the sample. These polarization shifts reflected pump-induced anisotropy in the substrate’s refractive index. For nanosecond-scale measurements in the near-infrared (NIR), a separate nanosecond TAS system was employed. Here, excitation was provided by 560 and 870 nm pulses from a Nd:YAG laser, while probe light came from a tungsten–halogen lamp. Transient NIR absorption spectra were recorded using a liquid nitrogen-cooled InSb detector, operating in single-channel mode with spectral scanning via a grating. Decay kinetics at each wavelength were captured using a Ni-Scope digital oscilloscope (8-bit, 100 MHz bandwidth, 30,000 data points).

Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy Measurements
The atomic force microscope (AFM) and Kelvin probe force microscope (KPFM) signals were detected by an SPM-9700HT (SHIMADZU, Japan) AFM instrument. The powder sample was dispersed in ethanol and then dropped on a Silicon chip. Au was used for the potentiometric calibration. CPD changes under dark and illumination were recorded to explore photoinduced charge dynamics. According to the following equation (1), the CPD can be calculated as:
CPD= ( sample − tip ) e−1 (1)
where sample is the work function of the sample, tip is the work function of the AFM tip.

In-situ DRIFTS characterization
In situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) measurement was performed on a Thermo Fisher Nicolet iS50 FTIR spectrometer equipped with a mercury-cadmium-telluride (MCT) detector cooled by liquid nitrogen and a DRIFTS accessory. Each spectrum was collected over the range of 4000 to 600 cm−1 at a resolution of 0.964 cm−1. The as-prepared samples were compressed at the bottom of an in situ ATR cell and then degassed for 1 h under an Ar atmosphere at 120 ℃ to remove the absorbed species before the photocatalytic experiments. After cooling down to room temperature, humidified CO2 (CO2/H2O = 4/1) was flowed into the specimen chamber to saturate the surface absorption of the catalyst. The DRIFTS spectra were collected after a certain irradiation duration. The simulated light source (UV-vis and UV-vis-NIR) was consistent with that in the photocatalytic experiment above.

Photocurrent and Mott-Schottky measurements
First, the original ITO glass was washed with acetone (30 min), ethanol (30 min), and water (30 min) using ultrasonic waves. The 5.0 mg catalyst was dispersed in 0.5 mL of ethanol and then treated with ultrasonic for 5 h. The obtained suspension was added to the 1.5 cm × 2 cm ITO glass drop by drop. Before the photoelectrochemical measurement, the ITO glass was treated in a vacuum at 150 ℃ for 2 hours. The CHI 660B electrochemical workstation equipped with three electrodes was used for photochemical experiments. An aqueous solution of 0.5 M Na2SO4 was used as the electrolyte. Using standard three electrodes, the catalyst-coated ITO was used as the working electrode, Pt foil was used as the counter electrode, and Ag/AgCl electrode was used as the reference electrode. The Mott-Schottky diagram was obtained at the frequencies of 1000 and 1500 Hz in the range of −1~1 V vs. Ag/AgCl.

Photocatalytic CO2 reduction measurement
The photocatalytic CO2 reduction experiments were carried out in a custom-made reactor with a quartz glass top (illuminated area approximately 1 cm²). 5 mg catalyst was uniformly spread on a glass fiber cloth after plasma cleaning and then placed into the reactor. Except for the temperature comparison experiment, all other experiments were conducted at room temperature (without any external heat source). A PLS-SXE300 Xe lamp (Beijing Perfect-Light Technology Co. Ltd.) with different reflectors and cut filters was used to simulate UV-vis, NIR, and full-spectrum. The light intensities can be adjusted continuously by changing the current of the xenon lamp and the optical path to the reactor. The light intensity on the sample surface was measured by an optical power meter (CEL-NP2000-2A, Beijing China Education Au-light Co., Ltd.), and the measuring range of wavelength was 190−11000 nm. Before irradiation, the whole reaction system was purged with CO2 and H2O vapor for 1 h to remove the gaseous impurity. High-purity CO2 was introduced into the reaction chamber through a mass flow controller, while H2O was injected into the chamber using a syringe pump, which can precisely control the amount of each reactant. The temperature of the catalyst bed was measured by a K-type thermocouple (DT-8891E) and an infrared thermometer (Fisher Scientific). The gas products were qualitatively detected using an Agilent GC-8890 gas chromatograph equipped with a TDX-01 column, a thermal conductivity detector (TCD), and a flame ionization detector (FID) with ultra-high purity argon as the carrier gas. The liquid products were quantified by a liquid chromatography (1260 Infinity II LC System, Agilent Technologies, Inc, Santa Clara, CA, USA) with a refractive index detector (RID) and a column from Bio-Rad.

To detect the difference between photothermal and traditional thermal catalysis, an IKA heating plate equipped with a thermocouple was used as a heat source for both the heating zone and reaction area to test the thermal catalytic activity.

Isotopic labeling experiments
13CO2 gas (isotopic purity 99%) was used as the carbon source instead of pure 12CO2 gas (chemical purity 99.999%), and the same photocatalytic process was used for isotope labeling measurement. The high-purity Ar was purged at a flow rate of 8 sccm for 60 min to remove any existing CO2 in the reactor. The reactor was then exposed to a 300 W Xe lamp for 1 h while continuously bubbling and stirring at a flow rate of 13CO2 and 12CO2 at 30 mL/min. Photocatalytic species were separated into individual substances via gas chromatography columns. The origin of products was analyzed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) (Trace 1310 GC-ISQ quadrupole MS, ThermoFisher, USA).

To confirm the oxygen source of O2, the labelled H218O experiment was performed as follows: CO2 was purged continuously into the reactor for 60 min. Then, 1 mL of H218O was introduced into the reactor. The temperature was controlled at room temperature. Then, the photocatalytic reaction experiment was conducted as before by irradiating the mixture for 1 h. The gas samples from the reactor were collected and analyzed by mass spectroscopy.

Equations evaluating photocatalytic CO2 reduction
The production rate, the selectivity, and the apparent quantum efficiency (AQE) were calculated as follows.
Production rate. The mass-normalized production rate of product i was calculated as55:
ri ( μmol g-1 h-1 ) = Ni / (mcat × t) (2)
where Ni is the amount of product i (μmol), mcat is the catalyst mass (g), and t is the irradiation time (h).

Amount of gaseous products. For continuous-flow analysis, the amount of product i was obtained from the outlet flow rate and the measured volume fraction:
Ni (mol)= (Fout × (Vi/100)) / Vm (3)
where Fout is the total outlet flow rate (sccm), Vi is the volume percentage of product i (vol%), and Vm = 22.414 L mol–1 is the molar volume of an ideal gas at 273.15 K and 1 atm.

Selectivity. The electron-based selectivity toward the product i was calculated as:
Si ( % ) = (ni × Ni) /  (nj × Nj) × 100% (4)
where ni is the number of electrons required to form one molecule of product i, and the summation index j refers to all detected reduction products.

Apparent quantum efficiency (AQE). The light was filtered by different monochromatic filters to test the PCOR, and the AQE was calculated as:
AQE ( % ) = (ne × Nprod) / Nph × 100% (5)
where ne is the electron number per product molecule (for CH4, ne = 8); Nprod is the amount of the target product formed (mol).
Nph = (I × A × t × ) / (h × c) (6)
where Nph is the total number of incident photons during the irradiation time t; I is the incident light intensity (W m–2); A is the illuminated area (m2); t is the irradiation time (s);  is the incident wavelength (m); and h and c are Planck’s constant and the speed of light, respectively.

COMSOL Multiphysics simulations
The finite element modeling (FEM)-based numerical framework in COMSOL Multiphysics 6.3 was used to numerically solve the frequency domain form of Maxwell’s equation:
 × (r−1  × E) − k02 (r − j / 0) E = 0 (7)
where k0 represents the wavenumber,  is the angular frequency, E is the scattered field; 0 is the vacuum permittivity, r, r, and  represent the properties of the material, namely, relative permeability, relative permittivity, and electrical conductivity, respectively.

The frequency domain module and thermal conduction module are coupled in one model, in which single spherical Bi@Fe2O3 nanoparticle is illuminated by the linear polarized plane wave, with a power density of 2.5 mW μm–2. The core radius and shell thickness of the Bi@Fe2O3 nanoparticle are 50 and 5 nm, respectively, in line with the TEM and SEM images. A spherical computational domain with a perfectly matched layer (PML) was implemented. To characterize the thermal effects of the plasma itself, the heat-transfer analysis was carried out by solving the steady-state form of the heat equation:
 Cp U T =  (k T) + q (8)
where T is the temperature, U is the velocity vector, k, , and Cp are the local properties, namely, thermal conductivity, density, and heat capacity, respectively. The heat source term q(r) induced by LSPR is given by the equation:
q(r) = 0.5  0 Im(r) |E(r)|2 (9)
where  is the angular frequency of the incident light, 0 is the vacuum permittivity of the material, and r is the complex relative permittivity, and E(r) is the local electric field. Optical constants and heat-transfer parameters for Bi, Fe2O3, and water were taken from the built-in Optical Materials Database. Due to the small length scale of the nanoparticle, the Grashof number is negligible, and the convective contribution to heat transfer can be neglected. Thus, heat transfer was modeled using the conduction equation in a sufficiently large domain that approximates an infinite medium.

Note: i) The perfectly matched layer (PML) is a non-reflective boundary condition that absorbs outgoing electromagnetic waves, minimizing spurious reflections to accurately model wave propagation in unbounded domains.
ii) Due to the high symmetry, only a quarter of the model is simulated to reduce computational costs.
iii) Due to the low air mass fraction, water’s properties are applied to the medium.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations
The spin-polarized first-principles calculations in this study were performed using density functional theory (DFT) as implemented in the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP, version 5.4.4)56. The interactions between valence electrons and ionic cores were described using the projector augmented wave (PAW) method57,58, which ensures accurate treatment of the core-valence interactions. The exchange-correlation energy was treated with the revised Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (RPBE) functional within the framework of the generalized gradient approximation (GGA)59. A kinetic energy cutoff of 500 eV was employed for the plane-wave basis set to ensure convergence of the total energy.

All structural optimizations were conducted using the conjugate gradient algorithm until the residual force on each atom was less than 0.05 eV/Å, and the electronic self-consistent field (SCF) convergence criterion was set to 10–6 eV. Brillouin zone integrations were carried out using a Γ-centered 2 × 3 × 1 Monkhorst-Pack k-point grid for the slab models. Gaussian smearing with a width of 0.05 eV was applied for electronic occupations. Where necessary, dipole corrections were applied to eliminate spurious interactions between periodic images. For surface and adsorption calculations, a vacuum layer of at least 15 Å was added along the direction perpendicular to the slab to avoid image interactions. To illustrate the long-range dispersion interactions between the adsorbates and catalysts, we employed the D3 correction method by Grimme et al60. All calculations were carried out under periodic boundary conditions.

The free energy change (G) of each elementary step was estimated using the following thermodynamic correction:
G = E + ZPE + T0 Cp dT − TS (10)
where E is the DFT total energy difference between initial and final states, ZPE is the zero-point energy correction, T0 Cp dT represents the thermal contribution to the enthalpy, and S is the entropy change. All thermodynamic corrections were obtained from vibrational frequency analysis and processed using the VASPKIT package61.

Note: It should be noted that although the experimentally synthesized Bi@Fe2O3 catalyst exhibits a core@shell architecture, constructing a full-scale core@shell model is hardly possible in DFT calculations. Therefore, as commonly reported in previous studies62-65, simplified slab-based models are employed to approximate the essential physicochemical features of core@shell systems. In a conventional stacked slab model (a layered “vertical” slab model, Supplementary Fig 57), the Bi/Fe2O3 interface is buried and inaccessible to reactant molecules, so that it is extremely difficult to investigate the interfacial electronic effects under CO2/H2O coexisting conditions. To better represent the realistic reaction microenvironment at the interface, a new Bi@Fe2O3 interfacial model was constructed by loading Bi nanoparticles onto the Fe2O3 slab. A layer of 16 H2O molecules was introduced above the surface to account for solvation and interfacial electric-field effects66.

Although this model represents a geometric simplification of the ideal core@shell structure, it captures the intrinsic electronic interaction at the Bi@Fe2O3 heterojunction. Importantly, the charge redistribution and activation mechanisms observed in this interfacial model reflect the intrinsic chemical nature of the Bi@Fe2O3 heterojunction. The resulting theoretical insights are therefore directly relevant to understanding the experimentally observed high selectivity for CO2 reduction to CH4 under CO2 and H2O coexisting conditions. Considering all computational constraints and mechanistic requirements, we believe that the adopted modeling approach provides more physically meaningful and experimentally consistent theoretical description of the catalytic mechanism proposed in this work.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

In this work, the authors synthesized a Bi@Fe2O3 core@shell structure and applied it to driven photoreduction of CO2 to CH4 under Uv-Vis-NIR light irradiation. The Bi@Fe2O3 obtained a CH4 production rate of 273.81 μmol g–1 h–1 with 98.6% selectivity. It is found that the Fe2O3 as a catalytic bed to accept the hot-electrons and confine the localized heat. This synergistic effect of photochemical and photothermal effects has achieved a result in the conversion of CO2 to CH4. Overall, the catalyst is well characterized and the system appears promising. However, there are a number of missing information and inconsistencies about mechanism for the catalytic procedure and selectivity that need to be addressed. Therefore, a major revision is suggested. Below are my comments and concerns.
1. The reduction of CO2 to CH4 is an 8-electron transfer process, which is significantly slower in kinetics compared to the pathway leading to CO formation. Why do current systems primarily detect CH4 as the main product while yielding minimal CO? In addition, the underlying mechanism lacks corresponding experimental validation.
2. The conduction band position of Fe2O3 is typically positive (more positive than 0 V vs. NHE), posing a significant thermodynamic challenge for driving CO2 reduction to CO or CH4. It is therefore difficult to reconcile this with the experimental observation that the authors detected these products on pristine Fe2O3. In contrast, if the product is originated from the hot electrons in Bi@Fe2O3, what’s the specific role of Fe2O3 in such a structure? The mechanism that overcomes this thermodynamic barrier needs to be addressed.
3. The authors propose that Fe2O3 functions as the photo-absorber while Bi provides LSPR-induced heat effect. However, under NIR light irradiation (which does not excite Fe2O3), a substantial CH4 yield (about 50% of the full-spectrum yield) is still observed on the Bi@Fe2O3. This notable NIR activity, which contradicts a mechanism solely dependent on Fe2O3's photo-absorption, remains unexplained.
4. Regarding the activity data, the authors have only provided the production rates for the reduction products (e.g., CH4, CO). For a complete assessment of the reaction, it is essential to also identify and quantify the oxidation products. Furthermore, what about the stoichiometry between the oxidation and reduction products?
5. The author claims an enhanced CO2 adsorption for the Bi@Fe2O3 core-shell composite compared to that of Fe2O3 and Bi-Fe2O3. However, if Bi is encapsulated as the core, the adsorption should be dominated by the shell properties. This apparent contradiction requires clarification.
6. The stability and potential evolution of the catalysts after reaction require further investigation. It is essential to characterize the post-reaction samples in terms of their morphology, composition, and chemical states. Analyses such as XRD, XPS, and TEM should be performed to confirm whether the core-shell structure remains intact, and to identify any potential phase transitions or changes in the oxidation states of Fe and Bi.
7. The stability of the Fe2O3 shell and the potential formation of bismuth oxide require thorough investigation. It is crucial to determine whether the surface defects of Fe2O3, proposed as active sites, are repaired or altered during the reaction. Concurrently, the chemical state of the Bi core must be verified to rule out its oxidation, which would fundamentally change the proposed LSPR and thermal mechanism.

### Reviewer 2

The study presents an innovative strategy for highly efficient, full-spectrum photocatalytic CO2 reduction PCO2R to CH4 using a noble-metal-free Bi@Fe2O3 coreshell nanostructure. The core concept of a "nanoscale greenhouse effect" is interesting to the community, enabling synergistic photochemical and photothermal catalysis by confining locally generated heat. The performance metrics, particularly the CH4 production rate and NIR-light AQE, are superior to current literature, making this work a significant contribution to sustainable energy and catalysis. The overall manuscript has been organized with good logic flow and well-written. However, before considering publication in the international edition of Nature Communications, we recommend the following minor revisions to enhance the clarity and rigor of the work.
1. Please ensure consistent terminology is used throughout the entire manuscript (including the main text and Supporting Information) when referring to the Bismuth components. For instance, standardize the usage to one term (e.g., sometimes Bi nanocore, sometimes Bi NCs, sometimes Bi NPs) instead of interchanging them..
2. The prominent defect visible in the upper-left corner of the Bi core in Figure 2E (main text) and Figure 2b (Supporting Information) is clearly noticeable. Please provide an explanation for the cause of this defect and discuss its potential impact, if any, on the catalyst's performance.
3. Supplementary Figure 14 shows that Bi-NC exhibits better light absorption properties, which are not presented in Figure 4a of the main text. Could you include this in Figure 4a and further analyze the mechanism behind the enhanced near-infrared absorption performance of 5-Bi@Fe2O3?
4. Figure 5 demonstrates the superior photocatalytic reduction performance of 5-Bi@Fe2O3. Could you include photocatalytic experiments under different atmospheres (N2, Air, pure CO2) for further comparison?
5. The in situ XPS clearly shows the formation of a higher concentration of Fe2+ under illumination, suggesting hot-electron trapping and the formation of oxygen vacancies are critical for CO2 activation. The final proposed mechanism (Fig. 6h/6i) primarily focuses on electron transfer. The authors must explicitly integrate the transient Fe2+ active site into the reaction mechanism, particularly for the activation of CO2 to the first intermediate (*COOH). Is the Fe2+ state the actual reaction site? Does the high temperature stabilize or destabilize this state?
6. What specific mechanism of the 5-Bi@Fe2O3 photocatalyst led to its selection in this study? Additionally, discuss the key differences between your core-shell system and previously reported photocatalytic dual-metal cases (e.g., AgCu bimetal photocatalyst in Ag2Cu2O3, or other bimetal photocatalyst), emphasizing the novelty of your "nanoscale greenhouse effect" strategy.
7. Supplementary Figures 6 and 7 display the physical adsorption capacity. Could you add the pore size distribution for Bi, Fe2O3, and Bi-Fe2O3, and further explain the influence of the core-shell structure of 5-Bi@Fe2O3?
8. The main text mentions that the specific surface area of the 5-Bi@Fe2O3 material has been enhanced. Please provide the BET data (table/figure) to quantitatively validate this claim.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript reports a Bi@Fe2O3 core-shell photocatalyst described as exhibiting a “nanoscale greenhouse effect” for full-spectrum CO2 reduction with H2O to CH4. The study is experimentally comprehensive, integrating fs-TA, KPFM, NAP-XPS, DRIFTS, and DFT analyses to correlate photothermal and photochemical contributions. The catalytic performance is impressive for a noble-metal-free system, and the proposed photothermal synergy represents a practical approach for harvesting the full solar spectrum for fuel production. Nevertheless, despite the solid experimental effort, the conceptual novelty and mechanistic interpretation require significant clarification. The current evidence for the proposed “nanoscale greenhouse effect” is not fully convincing, and several data inconsistencies, figure errors, and methodological gaps need to be addressed.
1. The manuscript attributes the higher temperature of Bi@Fe2O3 to an “infrared shielding” effect of the Fe2O3 shell. However, this description is too general and should specify the relevant infrared wavelength range. If the shell is proposed to “trap infrared heat,” the authors should clarify in which IR band this occurs and provide corresponding optical or thermal data (e.g., absorption or emissivity spectra) for Fe2O3. Without this information, the observed temperature increase is more plausibly due to enhanced broadband absorption or the low thermal conductivity of the shell rather than true infrared reflection or confinement. To further distinguish thermal confinement from electronic effects, the authors are encouraged to prepare a Bi@SiO2 reference sample. SiO2 is optically transparent and electronically insulating but provides similar thermal insulation owing to its low thermal conductivity. Comparing the heating behavior of Bi@Fe2O3 and Bi@SiO2 under identical illumination would help separate the pure photothermal (“greenhouse-like”) contribution from the electronic and catalytic roles of Fe2O3, thereby clarifying whether the observed temperature rise genuinely reflects an IR-shielding mechanism.
2. The size of the core-shell structure is mentioned more than once in the text ~100 nm. Is there any discrepancy between the text and the pictures? For example, in Figure 2c, the size is significantly larger than 200 nm.
3. There are numerous typographical and graphical errors throughout the manuscript. Please carefully check all figures and labels. Simulating the reaction pathways of CO2 and H2O coadsorption and activation at the Bi-Fe2O3 interface and comparing these results with those on bare Fe₂O₃ would provide a more realistic understanding of the catalytic mechanism and clarify the cooperative role of the Bi-Fe2O3 interface in the observed activity.

Comment 1: The reduction of CO to CH is an 8-electron transfer process, which is significantly slower in kinetics compared to the pathway leading to CO formation. Why do current systems primarily detect CH as the main product while yielding minimal CO? In addition, the underlying mechanism lacks corresponding experimental validation.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment regarding the fundamental kinetic challenge. We agree with the reviewer that the 8-electron reduction of CO to CH involves more complex steps and typically exhibits slower kinetics compared to the 2-electron pathway leading to CO formation.

However, in our work, pristine Fe O only yields an extremely small amount of CO (a 2-electron reduction product), and the formation of CH (requiring an eight-electron transfer) and H is negligible (Fig. R1a). This result indicates that, in the absence of sufficient driving force, the reaction is kinetically inclined to terminate at the CO stage due to the high energy barriers associated with the subsequent hydrogenation steps. It is worth noting that after introducing Bi nanoparticles, CH becomes the dominant product instead of CO (Fig. R1a). Importantly, after constructing the Bi@Fe O core@shell structure, the selectivity toward CH is markedly enhanced (Fig. R1a). This enhancement was ascribed to the unique role of the Bi core in providing a strong driving force to overcome these kinetic limitations.
Specifically, the Bi core contributes the driving force based on two synergistic effects: (i) high-energy hot electrons generated via localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) in Bi nanocaore possess a higher reduction potential than the intrinsic conduction band electrons of Fe O , which enable the reduction pathway to proceed beyond the *CO intermediate; (ii) a localized photothermal effect, which increases the local surface temperature and thereby accelerates the sluggish rate-determining hydrogenation steps (e.g., *CO → *CHO).

To further address the reviewer’s concerns and validate the mechanism in our work, we have performed additional experiments (in-situ DRIFTS and CO-TPD) and theory calculations (DFT). As shown in Fig. R2, Fig. R3 and Fig. R4, the evolution of surface intermediates over Fe O , Bi-Fe O , and 5-Bi@Fe O was monitored under full-spectrum irradiation. Upon irradiation, bands corresponding to *COOH and *CO intermediates were clearly observed over Bi-Fe O and 5-Bi@Fe O , while the peaks of these intermediates over Fe O are too weak to be almost unobservable. In contrast, the intensities of the intermediate-related peaks observed on Bi-Fe O are much lower than those detected on 5-Bi@Fe O . And key intermediates involved in CH formation, such as *CH O and *CH O, are almost undetectable on Bi-Fe O . While the subsequent emergence and strengthening of bands attributed to oxygen-bound intermediates such as *CHO, *CH O, and *CH O were observed on 5-Bi@Fe O . This indicates that the *CO species are strongly adsorbed to hydrogenate rather than desorbing as CO gas over 5-Bi@Fe O . In addition, CO temperature-programmed desorption (CO-TPD) measurements were performed to further investigate the CO adsorption strength on the surfaces of the three catalysts (Fig. R5). The 5-Bi@Fe O sample exhibits a CO desorption peak at a significantly higher temperature compared to pristine Fe O and Bi-Fe O , indicating a much stronger binding affinity for CO. Moreover, the projected crystal orbital Hamilton population (COHP) analysis exhibited that the spherical 5-Bi@Fe O catalyst exhibits a markedly more positive integrated COHP (ICOHP) value than the Fe O catalyst (3.92 eV vs 0.72 eV) (Fig. R6), indicating a stronger interfacial electronic coupling between the core@shell junction and the *CO intermediate. To further explore the mechanism underlying the high selectivity toward CO to CH over the core@shell structure, we calculated the Gibbs free energy diagrams for CO reduction pathways on the 5-Bi@Fe O and Fe O catalysts (Fig. R7). The hydrogenation of *CO to *CHO exhibits a higher energy barrier (0.98 eV) than that of CO desorption (0.20 eV) for Fe O catalyst, which indicates the *CO intermediate tends to desorb as CO gas instead of hydrogenation. So the construction of Bi@Fe O fundamentally alters the reaction pathway. The hydrogenation step from *CO to *CHO becomes thermodynamically downhill (–1.09 eV). This dramatic decrease in energy barrier means that once *CO is formed, it is spontaneously and rapidly protonated to *CHO rather than desorbing as CO gas. This “downhill” thermodynamic driving force effectively drives the reaction forward through the 8-electron pathway to CH .

Therefore, in our work, the high selectivity for CH originates from the unique property of the Bi@Fe O interface. The Bi core generates high-energy hot electrons via LSPR, which possess sufficient overpotential to drive the difficult multi-electron transfer steps that Fe O alone cannot sustain. And the localized heat confined by the Fe O shell significantly lowers the activation energy for the rate-determining hydrogenation steps (e.g., *CO → *CHO), effectively accelerating the deep reduction process. Consequently, the *CO intermediate is rapidly consumed (hydrogenated) on the surface rather than desorbing as CO gas, leading to more CH detection.
Finally, previous studies have demonstrated that product selectivity can depend upon reaction environment such as catalyst structure, sacrificial electron donor, and solvent media (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 2022, 61, e202116094; Inorg. Chem., 2015, 54, 5096-5104; Coord. Chem. Rev., 2018, 373, 333-356; Nat. Chem., 2020, 12, 180–185; Energy Environ. Sci., 2021,14, 2429-2440). Additionally, near-100% selectivity toward single products such as CH , C H , and CH COOH has been widely reported in recent photocatalytic CO reduction studies (Nat. Commun., 2024, 15, 4675; Energy Environ. Sci., 2024, 17, 5060-5069; Adv. Mater. 2025, e12480).
Thank you once again for your careful review and constructive feedback. We believe these revisions have significantly improved the manuscript’s readability and quality.

Comment 2: The conduction band position of Fe O is typically positive (more positive than 0 V vs. NHE), posing a significant thermodynamic challenge for driving CO reduction to CO or CH . Response: We thank the reviewer for this important comment. Firstly, we fully agree that the conduction band (CB) edge of bulk Fe O is generally located at a relatively positive potential (more positive than 0 V vs. NHE), which is thermodynamically unfavorable for CO reduction to CO/CH via a classical band-edge photoreduction mechanism. In the revised manuscript, we therefore clarify that the trace CO/CH detected on pristine Fe O should not be explained as arising from a pure CB-driven pathway. Moreover, we have provided a detailed explanation of the specific role of Fe₂O₃ in the core@shell architecture and made the corresponding supplement in the revised manuscript.
(i) Why can pristine Fe O show almost negligible PCO R activity?
The amounts of the detected products of PCO R over pristine Fe O catalyst in our experiments were extremely low (near the GC-MS quantification limit in our setup), which may be associated with defect-derived surface states and minor local heating rather than intrinsic band-edge reduction. Oxygen-vacancy-related defects are evidenced by EPR (Fig. R8a) and by the O 1s XPS deconvolution showing a distinct oxygen-vacancy component (Fig. R8b). These V surface defect states can locally enrich electrons (Fig. R8c), stabilize early activation intermediates (e.g., *COOH), and elevate surface temperature (Fig. R8d), enabling trace CO reduction under broadband irradiation even though the CB edge of bulk Fe O is not sufficiently negative (Fig. R9).
Moreover, very small amounts of PCO R products associated with non-band-edge processes, such as defect-related states, surface-trapped electrons, or localized thermal effects under illumination, have been reported in previous works (such as, J. Mater. Chem. A, 2021, 9, 22353-22363; Nano Lett., 2024, 24, 696-702).

Firstly, Fe O can modulate the electronic distribution at the core@shell interface. The ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) analysis and theoretical calculation results (DFT) indicate Bi has a lower work function than Fe O (Fig. R10a–c). As a result, the energetic hot electrons generated in the Bi NC can be efficiently transferred to the Fe O shell. This creates an electron accumulation layer (Fig. R10d), acting as an electron sink to efficiently extract and store hot electrons from Bi NC (Fig. R11). Because these are non-equilibrium interfacial hot electrons and trapped surface states, the CO reduction reaction is not strictly constrained by the CB position of bulk Fe O .

Moreover, the exposed Fe O shell provides a suitable reaction bed where CO adsorption, activation, and subsequent hydrogenation occur. In situ XPS over Bi@Fe O catalyst exhibited a substantially higher Fe2+/Fe3+ proportion than the Bi-Fe O catalyst (Fig. R12), consistent with the formation of electron-rich Fe-V sites O that facilitate the multistep proton-coupled electron transfer (as depicted in Fig. R13).

Finally, the shell acts as a thermal insulator to confine the LSPR-induced heat, which further lowers kinetic barriers for CO activation and intermediate hydrogenation. The Fe O shell in the core@shell structure effectively suppresses heat dissipation from the Bi core to the surrounding environment after illumination (as depicted in Fig. R14a). Consistently, temperature measurements show that 5-Bi@Fe O reaches markedly higher catalyst-bed temperatures than Bi-Fe O under identical illumination (Fig. R14b). COMSOL Multiphysics simulations further reveal obvious enhancement of local electric fields and surface thermal energy in 5-Bi@Fe O under near-infrared excitation, accompanied by a temperature increase of ~135 K (Fig. R14c). The resulting localized high-temperature environment promotes molecular collision frequency and reaction kinetics, thereby accelerating proton-coupled multi-electron steps required for CO -to-CH conversion.
In summary, the CO -to-CH conversion for Bi@Fe O is not limited by the band-edge position of the Fe O shell. Instead, plasmonic Bi supplies non-equilibrium hot electrons and localized nanoheating, while the exposed Fe O shell serves as the accessible catalytic bed that captures these hot electrons and provides Fe-V –associated O activation sites for CO adsorption, activation, and subsequent hydrogenation. The coupled effects of interfacial hot-carrier transfer, defect-mediated surface activation, and photothermal acceleration synergistically overcome the apparent thermodynamic barrier implied by the Fe O band edge, thereby enabling efficient CO activation and deep hydrogenation toward CH . We have revised the mechanistic discussion accordingly to clearly distinguish the intrinsic band-edge limitation of pristine Fe O from the actual operative pathway in Bi@Fe O .

Comment 3: The authors propose that Fe O functions as the photo-absorber while Bi provides LSPR-induced heat effect. However, under NIR light irradiation (which does not excite Fe O ), a substantial CH yield (about 50% of the full-spectrum yield) is still observed on the Bi@Fe O . Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that the activity of PCO R to CH under NIR irradiation cannot be explained by a mechanism solely relying on the photo-absorption of Fe O , because its bandgap does not allow direct excitation by NIR photons. We have revised the manuscript to clarify that CO was reduced to CH over Bi@Fe O via a photochemical-photothermal synergistic mechanism under NIR irradiation, in which NIR photons are utilized predominantly through plasmonic Bi even when Fe O is not directly photoexcited.

Under NIR irradiation, the Bi core is efficiently excited via localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR), as evidenced by the enhanced vis-NIR absorption of Bi-containing samples in the diffuse reflectance spectra (Fig. R15a). The plasmonic Bi generates non-equilibrium hot carriers, and the non-radiative relaxation of Bi plasmonic excitation creates strong localized photothermal effects, which are directly supported by the significantly higher catalyst-bed temperatures of 5-Bi@Fe O under illumination (Fig. R15b, c). The high-energy hot electrons produced in Bi core were injected into Fe O shell to directly participate in CO activation and reduction, bypassing the band-edge limitations of Fe O . Meanwhile, the localized temperature rise at the Bi/Fe O interface significantly accelerates the multi-electron proton-coupled steps required for CH formation. Accordingly, the robust NIR activity primarily originates from the synergy of plasmon-enabled hot-carrier and photothermal effects rather than Fe O bandgap excitation (explained in the Response to Comment 2).
Importantly, Fe O remains indispensable under NIR irradiation because it provides the catalytic reaction bed and CO activation sites. In situ XPS shows a clear illumination-induced Fe3+ → Fe2+ evolution (Fig. R15d), indicating that plasmon-derived hot electrons can be injected into the Fe O shell and trapped as defect-associated electrons. These Fe-V sites facilitate CO activation (e.g., * CO → O 2 2 *COOH) and promote deep hydrogenation steps toward CH . Therefore, even without direct Fe O photoexcitation, NIR-driven plasmonic hot-electron injection together with localized photothermal heating can activate CO and promote the multi-electron proton-coupled steps to CH formation.

It is noted that the difference between NIR irradiation and full-spectrum irradiation performance can be explained by the additional photochemical contribution under UV-visible irradiation. Under full-spectrum irradiation, Fe O can additionally contribute via bandgap excitation (UV-vis), supplying extra photogenerated carriers and further promoting the interfacial charge separation/transfer, while the Bi core still provides more photogenerated electrons and strong photothermal heating (Fig. R15 and Fig. R16), increasing the steady-state population of reactive carriers and key intermediates. As a result, the overall activity under full-spectrum irradiation is higher, whereas the NIR-only activity remains significant because the plasmonic hot-electron and photothermal effect alone already accounts for a large fraction of the total contribution.
In conclusion, the notable NIR activity does not contradict our mechanism; instead, this result is ascribed to a synergistic pathway. Here, plasmonic Bi core primarily supplies hot carriers and nanoheating, while Fe O acts as the catalytic reaction surface and provides Fe-V sites, enabling CO activation and deep reduction to CH . We thank the reviewer for this comment, which helped us refine and strengthen the mechanistic interpretation of the NIR-driven CO reduction behavior.

We fully acknowledge the reviewer’s concern about the oxidation products when studying photocatalytic CO reduction. Since our system was conducted in pure water without any sacrificial agents, identifying the oxidation products is indeed crucial to validate the source of electrons and protons (J. Mater. Chem. A., 2021, 9, 87-110; J. Am. Chem. Soc., 2023, 145, 422-435). As mentioned, pure water (H O) serves as the electron donor in our system, and CH was produced as the main product, along with trace CO and H . Therefore, the theoretical stoichiometric oxidation product is O (No other oxidized species were detected, such as H O ). In response to the key issues raised, we have carefully considered them and conducted further experiments to address these points.
We qualitate and quantify the O evolution by TCD detector in Agilent GC-8890 gas chromatograph under the calibration of standard pure O to monitor O evolution under the same photocatalytic conditions used for CH and CO quantification (Fig. R17a–c). In the experiment, argon gas was used as a carrier gas, and sample injection temperature and auxiliary heating temperature were set at 200 ℃ and 375 ℃, respectively, with the constant flow rate being 10 mL min-1. The initial temperature of the column box is 80 ℃, and the temperature is heated to 280 ℃ at 10 ℃ min-1, and the storage temperature is kept for 1 min. From the chromatographic signals analysis, the chromatographic peak observed at approximately 4–5 min can be attributed to O (Fig. R17c). Therefore, in this photocatalytic and photothermal-assisted reaction system, CO is reduced to CO and CH , while water is oxidized to O .
Fig. R17. (Supplementary Fig. 32, in the revised Supporting Information). (a) O production (oxidation product from water oxidation) over different samples as a function of time of irradiation in water. Error bars in these graphs represent standard deviations obtained from three independent measurements. (b) Mass spectrum of produced O under visible light over 5-Bi@Fe O catalyst. (c) Gas chromatogram of O in water over 5-Bi@Fe O catalyst.
To strictly assess the reaction stoichiometry, we performed a comprehensive electron balance analysis based on the detected production rates. The principle of charge conservation requires that the total rate of electrons consumed by the reduction half-reactions equals the rate of electrons released by the oxidation half-reaction.
The total electron consumption rate accounting for all reduction products (CH , CO, and H ) is calculated as:
Total reduction consumption electron = 8e– × R + 2e– × R + 2e– × R
CH4 CO H2
where R represents the production rate in PCO R.
The total electron generation rate from water oxidation to O is calculated as:
Total oxidation generation electron = 4e– × R
O2
Based on the gas chromatography data obtained from PCO R experiment (Fig. R17a), O evolution related to photogenerated holes consumption is stoichiometrically approximate to products of photogenerated electrons reduction (holes : electrons ≈ 1: 1). The slight deviation from the theoretical value is likely due to the strong adsorption of oxygen species on the catalyst surface or the H produced during the reaction reacted with O . This observation is consistent with many reported works (Nat. Commun., 2022, 13, 4592). These results together confirmed that the reaction in our system follows the theoretical stoichiometry of overall photocatalytic CO reduction with water.

Comment 2: The prominent defect visible in the upper-left corner of the Bi core in Figure 2E (main text) and Figure 2b (Supporting Information) is clearly noticeable. Please provide an explanation for the cause of this defect and discuss its potential impact, if any, on the catalyst's performance.
Response: We thank the reviewer for careful observation regarding the morphological details. The feature observed in the upper-left region of the Bi core in Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. 2b (Supplementary Fig. 3b, in the revised Supporting Information) may originate from the synthesis and core@shell formation process. Specifically, on the one hand, this feature observed in the morphology may be attributed to the anisotropic growth kinetics or volume contraction and interfacial strain induced during the encapsulation of the Bi core by the Fe O shell. On the other hand, it may result from minor localized etching at the Bi surface during the initial nucleation stage of the Fe O shell, which involves subsequent thermal treatment. Similar localized feature has been widely reported in metal-oxide core@shell systems formed under comparable conditions (Nat. Commun., 2025, 16, 7559; Nat. Commun., 2024, 15, 413; Adv. Mater., 2024, 36, 2406088; ACS Nano, 2022, 16, 5839−5850). Importantly, this defect does not compromise the structural integrity or continuity of the Bi core, nor does it disrupt the overall core@shell architecture. TEM analysis reveals that while such defects may appear locally, the majority of Bi cores maintain a well-defined morphology without extensive void formation or fragmentation.
Based on the results of PCO R, we emphasize that the feature observed in the morphology is not considered as the dominant active site responsible for the observed CO reduction activity. The catalytic performance in this work is ascribed to the synergistic interplay between photochemical and photothermal effects, which is evidenced by the consistent activity trends across the catalysts with varying local microstructural features. Moreover, the reproducible catalytic performance and narrow error bars obtained from multiple independent batches indicate that the activity is not sensitive to the presence or absence of such a feature.
Comment 3: Supplementary Figure 14 shows that Bi-NC exhibits better light absorption properties, which are not presented in Figure 4a of the main text. Could you include this in Figure 4a and further analyze the mechanism behind the enhanced near-infrared absorption performance of 5-Bi@Fe O ?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. Accordingly, we have included the UV-vis-NIR absorption spectrum of Bi NCs in Fig. R25, enabling a direct comparison with Fe O and 5-Bi@Fe O . The comparison clearly shows that while pristine Fe O has negligible absorption beyond 600 nm, both pure Bi NCs and 5-Bi@Fe O exhibit strong broadband absorption extending into the NIR region. The corresponding discussion has also been expanded in the revised manuscript.
Fig. R26 (Fig. 3a, in the revised manuscript) UV-vis-NIR DRS spectra of Bi NCs, Fe O , Bi-Fe O , and 5-Bi@Fe O .
The pronounced NIR absorption of the 5-Bi@Fe O core@shell structure is not only a superposition of the two components but involves a synergistic plasmonic effect. Specially, the broad NIR absorption originates from the Localized Surface Plasmon Resonance (LSPR) of the metallic Bi core. Unlike noble metals (Au/Ag) which resonate in the visible, the lower carrier density of Bi naturally positions its LSPR in the vis-NIR range. Crucially, coating the Bi core with an Fe O shell significantly modifies the plasmonic resonance. According to the Mie theory, the LSPR frequency is highly sensitive to the refractive index (n) of the surrounding medium. Fe O has a high refractive index (n ≈ 3.0 ). Encapsulating the Bi core in this high-dielectric shell induces a strong red-shift and broadening of the LSPR band compared to Bi in air/solvent, thereby enhancing the light harvesting capacity specifically in the NIR region (800–2000 nm).
In addition, the spherical core@shell geometry promotes multiple light-scattering and confinement effects, which increase the effective optical path length within the composite and further strengthen NIR light harvesting. Importantly, Fe O itself does not exhibit intrinsic near-infrared bandgap absorption. Instead, NIR photons are primarily absorbed by the plasmonic Bi core, generating hot carriers and localized photothermal effects, while the Fe O shell facilitates the interfacial transfer, confinement, and utilization of these plasmon-derived energetic carriers. Therefore, the 5-Bi@Fe O composite effectively integrates the NIR-harvesting capability of the Bi core, which is further optimized by the high-refractive-index Fe O shell, enabling efficient full-spectrum solar utilization.

Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. Following the reviewer’s recommendation, we have performed additional photocatalytic experiments under different atmospheres, including N₂, air, and pure CO (Fig. R27), under otherwise identical conditions (light intensity, catalyst mass, gas flow, and reaction time).
Fig. R27 The photocatalytic performance for 5-Bi@Fe O under different atmospheres.
Under N atmosphere, no detectable carbon-containing reduction products (CO or CH ) were observed for 5-Bi@Fe O , indicating that the detected products under CO atmosphere do not originate from residual carbon species or catalyst decomposition. The presence of CO is a prerequisite for fuel production. Based on the in situ XPS results (Fig. R29), combining other experimental and theoretical analyses in this work, we propose that the transient Fe2+ species generated under illumination (Fe3+ + e– → Fe2+) and oxygen vacancies adjacent to these species serve as the actual catalytically active centers (Fe-V sites) responsible for the initial CO activation and the subsequent hydrogenation steps. These Fe-V sites possess enhanced local electron density, which facilitate CO adsorption, molecular bending, and charge transfer into the antibonding orbitals of CO , thereby lowering the energy barrier for the formation of the first key intermediate (*COOH). The regenerated Fe2+ species continues to donate electrons to the surface-bound intermediates, driving the subsequent proton-coupled electron transfer steps (*COOH → *CO → *CHO → *CH O → *CH O → *CH ) (Fig. R31). Under continuous illumination, plasmon-induced hot-electron injection and localized photothermal heating sustain a dynamic Fe3+/Fe2+ redox cycle, ensuring persistent availability of Fe-V sites during multi-electron proton-coupled transfer steps toward CH formation.

Under operating conditions, the localized photothermal heating (∼220 °C) induced by plasmonic Bi does not lead to irreversible reduction or structural degradation of Fe O (Fig. R32). Instead, the elevated temperature promotes interfacial charge transfer, V -mediated electron trapping, and rapid Fe3+/Fe2+ redox cycling. As a result, the Fe-V sites are kinetically sustained under reaction conditions, enabling their persistent participation in CO activation rather than being thermodynamically stabilized or destroyed.

Comment 6: What specific mechanism of the 5-Bi@Fe O photocatalyst led to its selection in this study? Response: We thank the reviewer for giving us the opportunity to clarify our rational design and highlight the novelty of our strategy. The selection of this core@shell architecture was not empirical but was guided by a mechanism-oriented design strategy aimed at overcoming the intrinsic thermodynamic and kinetic limitations of CO reduction on Fe O .
Specifically, Fe O possesses abundant surface defects and strong CO affinity but suffers from an unfavorable conduction band position and limited light utilization. However, metallic Bi exhibits a broad LSPR response covering the vis-NIR region, enabling full-spectrum solar harvesting but lacks intrinsic catalytic activity toward multi-electron CO reduction. By constructing a Bi core fully encapsulated by a Fe O shell, the light harvesting, heat generation, and chemical activation were cooperatively coupled. In this system, the Bi core serves as a plasmonic nanoheater and hot-electron source, while the Fe O shell provides defect-rich catalytic sites and a confined reaction microenvironment (reaction bed).
Fig. R33. (Fig. 1, in the revised manuscript) Contrast of this work with previous works. Diagram illustrating the integration of intermittent sunlight and residual heat for on-demand CO conversion with water.
This design fundamentally differs from previously reported dual-metal or bimetallic photocatalysts (e.g., Ag-Cu systems), where performance enhancement is typically attributed to alloying effects, Schottky junctions, or static charge redistribution between adjacent metals. Additionally, due to high thermal conductivity of the alloy or bimetallic catalysts, the LSPR-generated heat is rapidly dissipated to the surroundings or the support, making it difficult to establish a high local temperature gradient (i.e., “heat is wasted”). In this work, the Bi@Fe O system exhibits a dynamic interfacial mechanism: plasmon-induced hot electrons and localized photothermal heating continuously generate and regenerate Fe-V active states on the interface between the Bi core and Fe O shell (Fig. R33). Importantly, the low thermal conductivity and closed geometry of the shell suppress heat dissipation, leading to a sustained local temperature elevation at the nanoscale.
Being similar to a greenhouse traps solar heat to maintain a warm earth, the Fe O shell traps the LSPR heat from the Bi core in this work. This synergistic light-heat-matter coupling was regarded as a “nanoscale greenhouse effect” which is fundamentally distinct from conventional photothermal enhancement or bimetallic charge transfer. Rather than only increasing carrier density or extending light absorption, this strategy creates a confined super-photothermal microenvironment that simultaneously accelerates reaction kinetics and stabilizes transient active states essential for deep CO reduction to CH . This provides a new paradigm for designing photothermal catalysts for photocatalytic CO reduction systems: moving from simple “light-to-heat conversion” to advanced “heat management and confinement”.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
General comment: This manuscript reports a Bi@Fe O core-shell photocatalyst described as exhibiting a “nanoscale greenhouse effect” for full-spectrum CO reduction with H O to CH . The study is experimentally comprehensive, integrating fs-TA, KPFM, NAP-XPS, DRIFTS, and DFT analyses to correlate photothermal and photochemical contributions. The catalytic performance is impressive for a noble-metal-free system, and the proposed photothermal synergy represents a practical approach for harvesting the full solar spectrum for fuel production. Nevertheless, despite the solid experimental effort, the conceptual novelty and mechanistic interpretation require significant clarification. The current evidence for the proposed “nanoscale greenhouse effect” is not fully convincing, and several data inconsistencies, figure errors, and methodological gaps need to be addressed.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer for the thorough evaluation of our manuscript and for acknowledging the comprehensive experimental and theoretical analyses. We also appreciate the reviewer’s constructive concerns regarding the mechanism of the proposed “nanoscale greenhouse effect,” as well as the noted figure inconsistencies. In response, we have revised the relevant sections to clarify the definition and physical origin of the nanoscale thermal confinement in the manuscript, combined with the additional experiments, numerical simulations, and DFT calculations. We have also carefully rechecked all data and figures to correct these inconsistencies. We address each specific comment point-by-point, with authors’ response in blue; changes to the manuscript in red. Detailed responses are given below:
1) New DFT model geometry to reflect the real composition of the Bi@Fe O core@shell structure.
2) The corrected size of the core@shell structure and other typographical and graphical errors throughout the manuscript;
3) The revised Fe 2p XPS peak-fitting diagrams;
4) XPS and XAFS for 5-Bi@Fe O photocatalyst before and after reaction;
5) New temperature measurements;
6) The new photocurrent data of all photocatalysts and the corresponding explanation;
7) Enhanced COMSOL Multiphysics simulations.
Comment 1: The manuscript attributes the higher temperature of Bi@Fe O to an “infrared shielding” effect of the Fe O shell. However, this description is too general and should specify the relevant infrared wavelength range. If the shell is proposed to “trap infrared heat,” the authors should clarify in which IR band this occurs and provide corresponding optical or thermal data (e.g., absorption or emissivity spectra) for Fe O . Without this information, the observed temperature increase is more plausibly due to enhanced broadband absorption or the low thermal conductivity of the shell rather than true infrared reflection or confinement. To further distinguish thermal confinement from electronic effects, the authors are encouraged to prepare a Bi@SiO reference sample. SiO is optically transparent and electronically insulating but provides similar thermal insulation owing to its low thermal conductivity. Comparing the heating behavior of Bi@Fe O and Bi@SiO under identical illumination would help separate the pure photothermal (“greenhouse-like”) contribution from the electronic and catalytic roles of Fe O , thereby clarifying whether the observed temperature rise genuinely reflects an IR-shielding mechanism.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. Following the reviewer’s recommendation, we have synthesized a Bi@SiO core@shell structure as a reference sample (Fig. R34a−d) and compared the heating behavior of Bi@Fe O and Bi@SiO under identical illumination. This additional comparison has helped us to explicitly decouple pure thermal confinement from electronic and catalytic effects, and refine the mechanistic description of the “nanoscale greenhouse effect”. We have revised the manuscript to clarify that the temperature enhancement in Bi@Fe O originates from nanoscale thermal confinement rather than selective infrared reflection.

Firstly, SiO is optically transparent across the UV-vis-NIR region (Fig. R34e and Fig. R34j) and electronically insulating. Bi@SiO exhibits an obvious temperature rise under illumination (Fig. R34f−i), confirming that the core@shell structure itself can induce photothermal confinement by suppressing heat dissipation from the plasmonic Bi core. This observation indicates that the temperature enhancement of Bi@SiO core@shell structure originates from a greenhouse-like thermal trapping effect at the nanoscale, rather than from selective infrared reflection.

(e) Thermal power generation and spatial distribution of temperature rise excited at an incident power density of 2.5 mW μm-2 of Bi@SiO . Scale bars, 50 nm.
Moreover, as shown in the UV-vis-NIR absorption spectra (Fig. R35a) and simulation transmittance spectra (Fig. R34j), 5-Bi@Fe O exhibits enhanced broadband absorption extending from the visible to the near-infrared region (300–2000 nm), which is primarily enabled by the plasmonic response of the Bi core. Importantly, Fe O itself does not act as an efficient reflector in any specific IR band. Instead, under illumination, the absorbed photon energy, particularly from the vis-NIR region, is predominantly converted into heat through non-radiative relaxation of plasmonically excited carriers. Therefore, the elevated temperature observed for Bi@Fe O is not attributed to infrared reflection but to suppressed heat dissipation (Fig. R35b). As shown in Fig. R35c, Bi@Fe O consistently reaches significantly higher steady-state temperatures than Fe O and Bi-Fe O under identical illumination conditions. Infrared thermal images (Fig. R35d) and COMSOL Multiphysics simulations (Fig. R35e) further confirm rapid heat accumulation and sustained temperature localization for the core@shell structure.
Importantly, however, a direct comparison reveals that the steady-state temperature achieved by Bi@Fe O is higher than that of Bi@SiO under the same irradiation intensity and spectral conditions (Fig. R34i and Fig. R35c). This result demonstrates that thermal confinement alone from the shell cannot fully account for the enhanced heating behavior of Bi@Fe O . In contrast to SiO , the Fe O shell enables strong interfacial electronic coupling with the Bi core, allowing plasmon-induced hot electrons to be injected into Fe O and subsequently trapped at Fe sites adjacent to oxygen vacancies. These electronic processes not only promote non-radiative energy dissipation but also dynamically generate Fe-V active centers, further reinforcing localized heat accumulation.
Therefore, we have replaced the term “infrared shielding” with “nanoscale thermal confinement” throughout the manuscript, which more accurately describes the plasmon-induced photothermal effect. Specifically, the observed temperature rise in Bi@Fe O reflects a synergistic photothermal-electronic process: the core@shell geometry provides nanoscale thermal confinement, while the semiconducting Fe O shell actively participates in trapping hot electrons and suppressing heat dissipation. We emphasize that this behavior is fundamentally different from passive thermal insulation, as demonstrated by the Bi@SiO reference. Accordingly, we have revised the manuscript to clarify that the “nanoscale greenhouse effect” originates from suppressed heat dissipation coupled with interfacial electronic interactions, rather than from a true infrared shielding or reflection mechanism.

Considering all computational constraints and mechanistic requirements, we believe that the adopted modeling approach provides more physically meaningful and experimentally consistent theoretical description of the catalytic mechanism proposed in this work.

“The density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to elucidate the thermodynamic origins of the enhanced activity and selectivity in the PCO R to CH over 5-Bi@Fe O . In specific, CO was adsorbed on the surface of 5-Bi@Fe O and Fe O to produce *CO , and then *CO was hydrogenated to produce *COOH. Owing to the high energy barrier, the first proton-coupled electron transfer for *COOH generation was considered a rate-limiting step. Importantly, the formation energy of *COOH on 5-Bi@Fe O is 0.67 eV, distinctly lower than that on pristine Fe O (0.85 eV), indicating that the electron-rich Bi/Fe O interface significantly decreases the energy barrier for CO activation. After that, *COOH was then protonated and dehydrated to form a stable intermediate *CO, which was associated with the C−O bond breakage through a proton-assisted electron transfer process50. After *CO formation, pristine Fe O tends to favor CO desorption rather than further hydrogenation (0.20 eV vs 0.98 eV). In contrast, the *CO intermediate is more strongly stabilized for 5-Bi@Fe O , and the subsequent hydrogenation to *CHO becomes thermodynamically preferred over CO desorption, thereby resulting in the pathway toward deep hydrogenation. The subsequent hydrogenation steps (*CHO → *CH O → *CH O → *+CH ↑) proceed with overall downhill energetics and small thermodynamic barrier, consistent with the enhanced CH selectivity. Notably, these theoretical trends are in good agreement with the experimental results. Specifically, the increased Fe2+/Fe3+ proportion under irradiation suggests an electron-enriched, defect-associated surface environment, while time-resolved DRIFTS shows the continuous accumulation of *CHO/*COOH-related bands on 5-Bi@Fe O . This is consistent with the predicted stabilization of key hydrogenation intermediates and the suppression of premature CO desorption. Therefore, the combined DFT and experiment analyses provide a clear logical framework for highly selective CH formation on the Bi@Fe O core@shell catalyst.”
